title: Đề luyện Đọc VSTEP — Recall RV0823 (4 passage)

passages.p1:
Harborview Furnishings is a mid-sized company that has sold furniture and household goods in the coastal town of Elmsford for almost forty years. What began as a single showroom above a hardware store is now a business with three branches, a busy workshop, and a small fleet of delivery vans. Over the decades, the company has built a reputation not only for the quality of its sofas, tables, and cabinets, but also for the wide range of services that come with them. For many local families, buying from Harborview has long meant far more than simply picking a product off a shelf and carrying it home.

At present, the company offers its customers a great deal beyond the sale itself. Trained advisers help shoppers plan how new pieces will fit into their rooms, while a small design team prepares detailed layouts for those redecorating an entire home. Once an order is placed, staff deliver the goods, assemble them on site, and take away old furniture at no extra cost. The workshop repairs damaged items and reupholsters worn ones, so that a favourite armchair need not be thrown away. Every purchase is backed by a generous warranty, and flexible payment plans allow customers to spread the cost over several months. These services, patiently refined over many years, are the main reason buyers have kept coming back.

Yet the managers of Harborview have grown uneasy. Sales in the showrooms have been flat for three years, and the typical customer is older than ever before. Younger shoppers, the directors have noticed, rarely set foot in the branches at all. Instead, they compare prices on their phones, read reviews late at night, and expect to arrange the whole purchase without speaking to anyone. Meanwhile, online-only rivals now deliver within a couple of days and provide clever tools that let buyers picture a chair in their own living room before ordering. In such a market, a firm that relies purely on its traditional strengths risks being quietly left behind, however loyal its existing customers may remain.

For these reasons, the board has agreed that the company must change the way it serves people rather than wait for trade to recover on its own. A redesigned website will let customers browse the full range, book a video consultation with a designer, and use a simple planning tool to arrange furniture inside a virtual copy of their own room. A rental scheme, aimed at students and young families who move house often, will offer good-quality pieces for a modest monthly fee. The firm also intends to introduce a line of goods made largely from recycled materials, responding to the many shoppers who now care deeply about the environmental cost of what they buy.

The directors believe these measures will do more than merely please the customers they already have. By meeting people where they now spend their time, online and on their phones, Harborview hopes to reach buyers who would never once have walked through its doors. The rental scheme in particular is designed to attract a younger audience early, in the expectation that renters who are happy with the service will, in time, become buyers of their own. Managing director Clara Nunes is careful, though, not to promise miracles. Technology on its own, she warns, wins nobody over; it is the human service behind it, delivered by staff who genuinely care, that will decide whether the company's next forty years prove as successful as its first.
passages.p2:
Social media has become woven into everyday life, yet not every platform attracts the same crowd. Two of the most widely discussed services, Facebook and Snapchat, show how differently online communities can be built. In a recent survey of internet users, roughly 68 percent said they used Facebook regularly, while only about 27 percent said the same of Snapchat. The gap grows even sharper when age is taken into account: nearly 60 percent of Snapchat's active users are under twenty-five, whereas Facebook draws steadily from every age group, including a large share of people over forty.

The material that people share on each platform reflects these different audiences. Facebook is often treated as a permanent record. Users post status updates, upload albums of photographs, announce major life events such as weddings or new jobs, share news articles, and join groups built around hobbies, neighbourhoods, or causes. Because most of this content stays visible indefinitely, people tend to present a relatively polished version of themselves, aware that friends, relatives, and even colleagues may scroll back through it months or even years later.

Snapchat works on almost the opposite principle. Its defining feature is that messages, photos, and short videos disappear soon after they are viewed, and 'Stories' vanish within twenty-four hours. This impermanence encourages a far more casual, spontaneous style. Instead of curating a flawless image, users send unedited snapshots of ordinary moments, frequently decorated with playful filters that add animal ears, cartoon effects, or amusing captions. The emphasis falls on sharing the here and now with a small circle of close friends rather than broadcasting to a wide audience.

Several factors explain why Snapchat has never matched Facebook's enormous reach. One is its narrow appeal. The application was plainly designed with teenagers and young adults in mind, and its gesture-based navigation, which hides many functions behind swipes and taps instead of clearly labelled buttons, can bewilder first-time or older users. Many people who try it briefly give up, complaining that they cannot work out how it operates. Older relatives, in particular, often conclude that the application was simply never meant for them, and quietly drift back to the services they already understand.

Another reason lies in the platforms' contrasting purposes. Facebook functions as an all-in-one hub: besides socialising, it lets people read the news, buy and sell goods in its marketplace, organise events, and run business pages. Snapchat, by contrast, stays focused almost entirely on private, moment-to-moment communication, so it simply serves fewer needs. Timing has also played a part. Facebook launched in 2004, years before Snapchat appeared in 2011, and by then it had already gathered hundreds of millions of members. Because a social network becomes more useful as more of one's contacts join it, this early lead proved hard to overturn. Finally, the very feature that makes Snapchat distinctive, its disappearing content, puts off some users, who would rather keep a lasting archive of their memories than send messages that erase themselves.

In the end, neither platform is simply better than the other; they answer different desires. Facebook rewards those who want a durable, wide-ranging network and a stored history of their lives, while Snapchat appeals to younger people looking for quick, informal exchanges that leave no trace. Their contrasting fortunes suggest that in the crowded world of social media, success depends not only on arriving first but on matching a design to what a broad audience genuinely wants.
passages.p3:
In much of the Americas, a name is rarely a neutral label. It is a compact biography, a set of coordinates that strangers use to place a person before a single word has been exchanged. Long before the immigration histories of the New World turned surnames into archaeological records of arrival, philosophers had insisted that naming was an act of power. What the modern era has added is scale. Today a name is not merely whispered across a dinner table; it is ingested by databases, ranked by algorithms, and cross-checked against rosters that decide who is seen and who is quietly passed over.

Consider the case of Mai-Claire Bennett, a Vietnamese-American woman born and raised in a mid-sized city in the American South. Her passport affirms her citizenship without qualification, yet her name, half English and half Vietnamese, has spent her whole life refusing to sit comfortably in any single box. Her parents had argued over it for weeks before she was born. Her father, weary of watching relatives anglicize themselves into invisibility, wanted a Vietnamese given name; her mother feared the small, daily frictions such a name would invite. The hyphen was their compromise, a bridge they hoped would let their daughter belong to both shores at once.

The bridge, it turned out, had a structural flaw that no one had anticipated. In her final year at university, Mai-Claire was nominated for a competitive national fellowship whose selection committee verified each candidate's academic record by running an automated match against transcripts held by partner institutions. Over the years her name had been recorded in half a dozen incompatible ways: as Mai Claire Bennett on one registrar's form, as Mai C. Bennett on another, as Bennett, Mai-Claire in a database that could not accommodate the hyphen. When the fellowship's software searched for a single, exact string, it found nothing. No human paused to ask why. She was quietly dropped from the shortlist, and only a chance email months later revealed that the omission had been clerical rather than merited.

Her experience is a particularly vivid instance of a phenomenon researchers have documented for decades. Field experiments in which identical resumes are dispatched under different names have repeatedly shown that applicants whose names read as foreign, or as belonging to a marginalized group, receive markedly fewer callbacks than those whose names sound reassuringly familiar. The bias is rarely conscious and almost never admitted; it operates in the split second before deliberation, in the flicker of assumption a name triggers. What made Mai-Claire's case unusual was not the presence of prejudice but its absence. No one had judged her name unworthy. A machine had simply failed to read it, and its silence was taken for hers.

The Americas make an especially revealing laboratory for such failures. Few regions have absorbed so many naming traditions, and fewer still have designed their institutions to accommodate them. In much of Latin America, a person carries two surnames, one inherited from each parent, a convention that routinely bewilders forms built on the Anglo assumption of a single family name. Databases truncate the second surname, file it as a middle name, or discard it altogether, so that a woman named for both her lineages can be rendered, by an unthinking template, into someone she is not. The tidy North American grid of first name, middle initial, and last name is not a universal fact of human identity; it is a local custom that has quietly been promoted to the status of a standard.

To surrender to that standard is to accept a bargain many immigrant families know intimately. An anglicized name lubricates the machinery of daily life; it spares its bearer the mispronunciations, the raised eyebrows, the small delays at every checkpoint of a bureaucratic society. Yet the same smoothing erases the very inheritance a name is meant to transmit. A name is one of the few possessions a family can hand down without cost and without diminishment, a thread connecting a child to grandparents she may never have met and to a language she may never learn to speak. To trade it away for convenience is to make a payment whose true price is not visible until much later.

None of this is to romanticize the hyphen, which solves one problem while creating others, nor to suggest that every clerical error conceals a moral failing. The lesson of Mai-Claire's near-erasure is subtler and, in a way, more unsettling. It is that the systems we build to be neutral inherit the assumptions of those who build them, and that a person can be overlooked not because anyone decided she did not belong, but because no one designed the machinery to notice that she did. In a hemisphere assembled from the names of the whole world, that is a costly oversight, and it is one that falls, as such costs usually do, on the person least able to see it coming.
passages.p4:
For all its resemblance to timber, bamboo is not wood at all. It belongs to the grass family, a botanical curiosity that places this towering plant in the same lineage as wheat and rice rather than oak or teak. What looks like a trunk is in fact a culm, a hollow, segmented stem that shoots upward from an underground network of roots known as a rhizome. Native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, Africa and Latin America, bamboo thrives in warm, humid climates where rainfall is plentiful, and it colonises open ground with a tenacity that few cultivated species can match. A single clump, left undisturbed, spreads outward season after season, sending up fresh culms from the same root system without ever needing to be replanted.

It is this manner of growth that first commends bamboo to anyone weighing it against conventional timber. Whereas a hardwood such as oak may take fifty years or more to reach a size worth felling, certain bamboo species attain their full height within a single growing season, some varieties lengthening by nearly a metre in a day under ideal conditions. Because harvesting a mature culm does not kill the plant, since the rhizome simply pushes up a replacement, a well-managed stand can be cropped every three to five years almost indefinitely. Where a felled forest leaves behind a scarred clearing that will not recover for decades, a bamboo grove regenerates almost as quickly as it is cut. For manufacturers under pressure to prove a steady, renewable supply, this rhythm of near-continuous yield is difficult to ignore.

The plant's appeal, however, extends well beyond the speed at which it grows. Pound for pound, the fibres running the length of a culm give bamboo a tensile strength, its resistance to being pulled apart, that rivals or even exceeds that of mild steel, a property that has earned it the nickname 'vegetal steel' among engineers. Its hollow, ringed structure marries lightness with a stiffness that makes it a natural candidate for flooring, panelling and even load-bearing beams once it has been sliced, laminated and pressed into engineered boards. Bamboo is also a voracious absorber of carbon dioxide, and a fast-growing grove locks away atmospheric carbon at a rate that outpaces many broadleaf forests of comparable area, at least while the plants are young and growing vigorously. In an age preoccupied with emissions, that capacity has become a powerful selling point.

Taken together, these attributes explain why builders and furniture makers have increasingly turned to the grass in place of slower-growing wood. The commercial logic is straightforward. As tropical hardwoods grow scarcer and the felling of old-growth forest attracts ever fiercer criticism, a material that reaches maturity in a few seasons, on marginal land unsuited to food crops, offers a way to satisfy demand without stripping ancient woodlands. Bamboo is frequently cheaper to cultivate than plantation timber, and it lets a company advertise its wares as environmentally responsible, a label that carries growing weight with buyers. For an industry anxious about both supply and reputation, the grass appears to solve two problems at once.

Yet the enthusiasm surrounding bamboo deserves to be tempered by a clear-eyed look at its shortcomings. In its natural state the culm is prone to attack by insects and fungi and readily absorbs moisture, so it must be treated or chemically stabilised before it can be trusted in a damp climate. More troubling, the process of turning raw stalks into the smooth, uniform boards sold in showrooms leans heavily on adhesives, and cheaper resins can release formaldehyde, a compound linked to poor indoor air quality, long after installation. Converting a hollow stem into a dense engineered panel is, in addition, an energy-hungry undertaking, since the shredding, boiling, drying and pressing consume electricity and heat that erode part of the carbon advantage the plant enjoys in the field.

Distance compounds the problem. The overwhelming majority of commercial bamboo is grown and processed in Asia, so a floor laid in Europe or North America may have travelled thousands of miles by ship before reaching the buyer, and those shipping emissions must be set against whatever the plant saved while it was growing. None of this negates bamboo's genuine promise; it simply cautions against the sweeping claims that too often accompany it. Whether the grass truly earns its green reputation depends less on the plant itself than on how, and how far, it is grown, treated and transported. Handled thoughtfully, bamboo may genuinely lighten the load that our appetite for timber places on the world's forests; marketed carelessly, it risks becoming one more product whose environmental halo shines brighter than its actual record.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What is Harborview Furnishings?
options: A. A recently launched company that sells its furniture only through its website.
B. A large national chain that specialises in selling hardware and building supplies.
C. A medium-scale retailer that has sold home furniture for nearly four decades.
D. A family workshop that does nothing except repair and reupholster old pieces of furniture.
questions.explanation: Bài mở đầu bằng 'mid-sized company that has sold furniture and household goods... for almost forty years', tức doanh nghiệp tầm trung bán nội thất gần 40 năm, nên C đúng (diễn đạt lại 'mid-sized'='tầm trung', 'almost forty years'='gần bốn thập kỷ').

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

According to the passage, what does Harborview do once a customer has placed an order?
options: A. They deliver and put together the new pieces, then remove the old furniture free of charge.
B. They lend customers all the tools and instructions they need to assemble the furniture themselves.
C. They provide a full cash refund to any customer who is unhappy with the finished design.
D. They store the furniture in their warehouse without charge until the customer's new home is finally ready.
questions.explanation: Bài nêu 'staff deliver the goods, assemble them on site, and take away old furniture at no extra cost', nên A đúng (giao, lắp ráp, mang đồ cũ đi không tính phí).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

In paragraph 3, the word 'flat' (in 'Sales... have been flat') is closest in meaning to sales that...
options: A. have fallen suddenly and quite steeply
B. have become increasingly hard to predict
C. have at last begun to climb again
D. have stayed at roughly the same level
questions.explanation: 'Sales in the showrooms have been flat for three years' nghĩa là doanh số không tăng, giữ nguyên một mức; ngữ cảnh sau đó (ban lãnh đạo bất an, khách già đi) xác nhận đây là trạng thái đi ngang, nên D đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

Why have the managers of Harborview become uneasy about the company's future?
options: A. Their most experienced advisers and designers have recently begun to resign in numbers.
B. Growth has stalled and they are failing to attract younger, digitally-minded buyers.
C. Maintaining the delivery vans and the busy workshop has grown far too costly.
D. Their loyal older customers have recently started complaining about the declining service.
questions.explanation: Bài cho biết doanh số 'flat for three years', khách 'older than ever' và người trẻ 'rarely set foot in the branches' vì họ mua sắm qua điện thoại, nên B (tăng trưởng chững lại, không hút được khách trẻ chuộng số hoá) đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does the passage say the design team does?
options: A. It draws up detailed plans for people redecorating their whole home.
B. It visits each customer's house in order to measure every room in person.
C. It runs classes that teach customers how to build their own furniture.
D. It selects the paint colours and the lighting to suit each room.
questions.explanation: Bài nêu 'a small design team prepares detailed layouts for those redecorating an entire home', nên A đúng ('layouts'='bản vẽ chi tiết', 'entire home'='toàn bộ ngôi nhà').

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

According to the passage, why do online-only rivals have an advantage?
options: A. They sell identical products at far lower prices than Harborview does.
B. They provide much longer warranties and far more generous instalment plans.
C. They operate showrooms in far more towns right across the country.
D. They combine rapid delivery with tools for imagining items at home.
questions.explanation: Bài nói đối thủ 'deliver within a couple of days and provide clever tools that let buyers picture a chair in their own living room', nên D đúng (giao nhanh cộng công cụ giúp hình dung sản phẩm).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What is the main purpose of the new rental scheme?
options: A. To clear out the old stock that has stayed unsold in the branches.
B. To win over mobile young customers who may later become buyers.
C. To replace the firm's existing payment plans with a single fixed option.
D. To bring in some extra income while showroom sales remain flat.
questions.explanation: Bài nói chương trình cho thuê 'designed to attract a younger audience early, in the expectation that renters... become buyers', tức thu hút khách trẻ để về sau họ thành khách mua, nên B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

All of the following are services Harborview CURRENTLY offers EXCEPT...
options: A. repairing customers' damaged pieces and re-covering the ones that have worn out.
B. backing every single purchase with a generous warranty.
C. renting out furniture to customers in return for a regular monthly payment.
D. letting customers pay for their orders in instalments across several months.
questions.explanation: Cho thuê nội thất là kế hoạch TƯƠNG LAI ('A rental scheme... will offer...'), chưa phải dịch vụ hiện có, nên C là đáp án NGOẠI TRỪ. A/B/D đều được nêu là dịch vụ đang có (repairs/reupholsters, warranty, payment plans).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What can be inferred about Harborview's traditional services?
options: A. They are the chief reason younger shoppers now avoid the company.
B. They will be dropped altogether as soon as the new website goes live.
C. They now matter more to the firm's success than at any earlier time.
D. They remain valuable but are no longer sufficient on their own.
questions.explanation: Dịch vụ truyền thống từng khiến khách quay lại, nhưng bài cảnh báo nếu công ty 'relies purely on its traditional strengths' thì 'risks being quietly left behind', hàm ý chúng vẫn giá trị nhưng đã không còn đủ, nên D đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What is Clara Nunes's attitude towards the planned changes?
options: A. She is certain that technology by itself will secure future success.
B. She is hopeful but measured, valuing caring staff above technology alone.
C. She firmly opposes the plans and would rather keep the old methods.
D. She feels indifferent, doubting the result can be shaped at all.
questions.explanation: Nunes 'careful... not to promise miracles' và cảnh báo 'Technology on its own... wins nobody over; it is the human service behind it... that will decide', cho thấy thái độ vừa hy vọng vừa thận trọng, đề cao yếu tố con người, nên B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

According to the survey mentioned in the passage, how did Facebook's usage compare with Snapchat's?
options: A. Around a quarter of respondents used Facebook, while roughly two thirds used Snapchat.
B. Nearly two thirds of respondents used Facebook, more than double the share using Snapchat.
C. Both platforms were used by a similar share, close to half of those asked.
D. Snapchat was used by just over a quarter, and Facebook by only a slightly larger share.
questions.explanation: Bài nêu 'roughly 68 percent... used Facebook' và 'only about 27 percent' dùng Snapchat; 68% xấp xỉ hai phần ba và hơn gấp đôi 27%, nên B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

Which of the following best describes the content that people usually post on Facebook?
options: A. Brief clips and images that are meant to be seen only once.
B. Private messages shared only with a small handful of close friends.
C. Lasting updates and photographs that remain available to look back on later.
D. Only formal business reports and official documents of a professional kind.
questions.explanation: Bài viết 'most of this content stays visible indefinitely' và người dùng đăng status, album ảnh, sự kiện; C diễn đạt lại ý nội dung lưu lâu để xem lại.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What does the passage present as the most distinctive characteristic of Snapchat?
options: A. Its content is short-lived and removes itself after a brief time.
B. It keeps a permanent copy of every message for later reference.
C. It is used mainly for reading the news and purchasing goods.
D. It permits only written text and blocks all images and video.
questions.explanation: Bài nêu 'messages, photos, and short videos disappear soon after they are viewed'; A diễn đạt lại đặc điểm nội dung tự biến mất.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

The passage says that Snapchat users often decorate their snaps with filters that add:
options: A. detailed background information about where each photo was taken.
B. permanent watermarks that prove who originally took the image.
C. professional editing tools intended for polished photography.
D. lighthearted touches such as cartoon-like features and funny captions.
questions.explanation: Bài mô tả 'playful filters that add animal ears, cartoon effects, or amusing captions'; D diễn đạt lại thành nét vui tươi kiểu hoạt hình và chú thích hài hước.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What can be inferred from the fact that nearly 60 percent of Snapchat's active users are under twenty-five?
options: A. Almost no one above the age of twenty-five knows that Snapchat exists.
B. Younger people make up the greater part of the platform's active audience.
C. Snapchat has more users than Facebook among teenagers in particular.
D. Exactly 40 percent of Snapchat's users are middle-aged working adults.
questions.explanation: Từ 'nearly 60 percent of Snapchat's active users are under twenty-five' suy ra người trẻ chiếm phần lớn người dùng tích cực, nên B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

In paragraph 3, the word 'impermanence' is closest in meaning to:
options: A. the quality of being temporary and not lasting.
B. the difficulty of learning how to use something.
C. the power to reach an extremely large audience.
D. the habit of carefully polishing one's public image.
questions.explanation: Ngữ cảnh 'This impermanence' gắn với việc nội dung 'disappear' và 'vanish within twenty-four hours', tức tính tạm thời không bền lâu, nên A đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

Why, according to the passage, was Facebook's early start so hard for Snapchat to overcome?
options: A. Snapchat had in fact launched earlier than Facebook and then quickly lost momentum.
B. Facebook had poured far more money into advertising campaigns than its younger rival.
C. Young users had initially disliked both of the platforms in roughly equal measure.
D. A network gains value as more of a user's own contacts already use it.
questions.explanation: Bài giải thích 'a social network becomes more useful as more of one's contacts join it', nên lợi thế sớm khó lật ngược; D diễn đạt lại ý hiệu ứng mạng lưới.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

The passage gives all of the following as reasons for Snapchat's smaller user base EXCEPT:
options: A. its interface, based on swipes and taps, confuses new or older users.
B. it satisfies fewer needs because it focuses only on private, in-the-moment sharing.
C. it charges a monthly subscription fee that discourages potential newcomers.
D. some people dislike that its content deletes itself instead of being kept.
questions.explanation: A, B, D đều là lý do có trong bài (giao diện vuốt chạm, đáp ứng ít nhu cầu, nội dung tự xóa); bài KHÔNG hề nhắc tới phí thuê bao, nên C là đáp án NGOẠI TRỪ.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What does the passage imply about why Facebook users tend to present a 'relatively polished version of themselves'?
options: A. They are required by Facebook's rules to keep their profiles formal and tidy.
B. They know a durable record may later be reviewed by a wide range of people.
C. They want to attract as many strangers and new followers as they possibly can.
D. They find the platform's editing filters make each of their posts look professional.
questions.explanation: Bài nói người dùng chỉn chu vì nội dung 'stays visible indefinitely' và 'aware that friends, relatives, and even colleagues may scroll back'; B nắm đúng hàm ý hồ sơ lâu dài bị nhiều người xem lại.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

Which statement best captures the author's overall attitude toward the two platforms?
options: A. Facebook is clearly the superior platform and will soon replace Snapchat entirely.
B. Snapchat's fresh approach makes it the more promising of the two platforms.
C. Both platforms are gradually losing their relevance to newer rival services.
D. Neither is truly better, since each one suits a different set of user needs.
questions.explanation: Kết bài khẳng định 'neither platform is simply better than the other; they answer different desires', nên D phản ánh đúng thái độ trung lập của tác giả.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

According to the passage, Mai-Claire's status as a citizen of the United States is
options: A. still awaiting confirmation from the authorities.
B. conditional on which form of her name she uses.
C. firmly established and not in question.
D. a privilege she obtained through the fellowship.
questions.explanation: Câu 'Her passport affirms her citizenship without qualification' nghĩa là quốc tịch được khẳng định không chút dè dặt, tức vững chắc và không phải bàn cãi (đáp án C).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Why did Mai-Claire's parents give her a hyphenated name?
options: A. To reconcile their two differing wishes for her.
B. To make her name easier for officials to record.
C. To follow a common Vietnamese-American custom.
D. To honour a relative who had anglicized her name.
questions.explanation: 'The hyphen was their compromise' giữa người cha (muốn tên Việt) và người mẹ (sợ phiền toái) nên đáp án A 'dung hoà hai mong muốn khác nhau' là đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

What was the immediate cause of Mai-Claire being removed from the fellowship shortlist?
options: A. The committee doubted the authenticity of her transcripts.
B. Reviewers considered her academic record insufficient.
C. Her partner institutions refused to release her records.
D. Software failed to match her inconsistently recorded name.
questions.explanation: Tên cô được ghi 'in half a dozen incompatible ways' và phần mềm 'searched for a single, exact string, it found nothing', nên đáp án D.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

In the sentence 'A machine had simply failed to read it, and its silence was taken for hers,' the word 'hers' refers to the silence attributed to
options: A. the machine that processed her records.
B. the fellowship's selection committee.
C. Mai-Claire herself.
D. her parents, who named her.
questions.explanation: 'its' là sự im lặng của cỗ máy (không trả về kết quả), bị hiểu nhầm thành 'hers', tức sự im lặng của chính Mai-Claire, như thể cô không dự tuyển hay không đủ tư cách, nên đáp án C.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

According to the passage, the two-surname convention common in Latin America causes problems because
options: A. Latin Americans frequently change their surnames.
B. many official forms assume a person has only one surname.
C. the two surnames are difficult to pronounce correctly.
D. databases store the surnames in the wrong language.
questions.explanation: Bài viết 'a convention that routinely bewilders forms built on the Anglo assumption of a single family name', tức nhiều biểu mẫu mặc định chỉ một họ, nên đáp án B.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

The passage mentions all of the following ways that databases mishandle a second surname EXCEPT
options: A. cutting it short.
B. treating it as a middle name.
C. leaving it out entirely.
D. translating it into English.
questions.explanation: Ba cách bài nêu là 'truncate' (cắt cụt), 'file it as a middle name' (xếp thành tên đệm) và 'discard it altogether' (loại bỏ hoàn toàn); 'dịch sang tiếng Anh' KHÔNG được nhắc nên là đáp án đúng của câu EXCEPT (D).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the bureaucratic systems discussed in the passage?
options: A. Indifferent, since such errors are too rare to matter.
B. Critical of their unintended exclusions, without alleging deliberate malice.
C. Admiring of their efficiency despite occasional flaws.
D. Outraged at the deliberate discrimination they enact.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối viết hệ thống 'inherit the assumptions of those who build them' và người ta bị bỏ sót 'not because anyone decided', cho thấy tác giả phê phán sự loại trừ vô tình mà không quy ác ý, nên đáp án B.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

It can be inferred from the passage that immigrant families who anglicize their names
options: A. trade a lasting inheritance for short-term practical ease.
B. usually come to regret the decision within a few years.
C. do so mainly to improve their children's job prospects.
D. are rejecting their heritage out of shame.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 6 nói tên Anh hoá 'lubricates the machinery of daily life' nhưng 'erases the very inheritance' và cái giá 'not visible until much later', nên suy ra: đổi di sản lâu bền lấy tiện lợi trước mắt (A).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Which of the following best summarizes the central argument of the passage?
options: A. A person's name is the single greatest determinant of their success in life.
B. Immigrants ought to keep their heritage names despite every difficulty this creates.
C. Latin American naming customs are considerably richer than North American ones.
D. Seemingly neutral systems can exclude people by encoding narrow assumptions, causing harm without intent.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối chốt: hệ thống dựng để trung lập 'inherit the assumptions of those who build them' và người bị bỏ sót dù 'no one decided', nên D tóm đúng luận điểm.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

In the phrase 'An anglicized name lubricates the machinery of daily life,' the word 'lubricates' most nearly means
options: A. complicates.
B. eases.
C. conceals.
D. controls.
questions.explanation: Ngữ cảnh 'lubricates the machinery of daily life' cùng ý 'spares its bearer the mispronunciations ... small delays' cho thấy 'lubricates' nghĩa là làm cho dễ dàng, trơn tru (B).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

According to the passage, bamboo is best described as:
options: A. A fast-growing tree native to the tropics.
B. A tropical hardwood prized for its strength.
C. A grass that people use in place of wood.
D. A hybrid of grass and hardwood species.
questions.explanation: Bài mở đầu: 'bamboo is not wood at all. It belongs to the grass family' và các đoạn sau cho thấy tre được dùng như gỗ, nên C đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

In paragraph 1, why can a clump of bamboo keep producing new stems without being replanted?
options: A. New culms grow from its underground root system.
B. It is watered by heavy tropical rainfall.
C. Its seeds scatter and germinate around the parent plant.
D. Each culm splits to form several new stems.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 1: 'sending up fresh culms from the same root system without ever needing to be replanted', lóng mới mọc từ thân rễ ngầm, nên A đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

How does harvesting bamboo differ from felling a hardwood forest, according to paragraph 2?
options: A. Bamboo can be harvested only once every fifty years.
B. Cutting bamboo, like cutting oak, leaves a clearing that recovers slowly.
C. Bamboo never needs to be cut because it renews itself automatically.
D. The plant survives cutting, so one stand can be harvested repeatedly.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 2: 'harvesting a mature culm does not kill the plant... a well-managed stand can be cropped... almost indefinitely', chặt lóng không giết cây nên khai thác lặp lại được, D đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

Why do engineers refer to bamboo as 'vegetal steel'?
options: A. Because it is as heavy and dense as metal.
B. Because it withstands stretching forces as well as, or better than, mild steel.
C. Because it is manufactured together with steel in beams.
D. Because it is stronger than every material now in use.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 3: tre có 'a tensile strength... that rivals or even exceeds that of mild steel', sức chống lực kéo sánh với thép, nên có biệt danh 'thép thực vật', B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

The passage mentions all of the following as drawbacks of bamboo EXCEPT:
options: A. Untreated culms can be damaged by insects and moisture.
B. The glues used in processing can give off harmful fumes.
C. Its cultivation competes with farmland needed for food crops.
D. Turning stalks into boards consumes a great deal of energy.
questions.explanation: Ba nhược điểm ở đoạn 5-6 (sâu mọt/ẩm, keo thải formaldehyde, ngốn năng lượng). Tranh đất trồng lương thực KHÔNG được nêu, bài còn nói tre trồng trên 'marginal land unsuited to food crops', nên C là ngoại lệ.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

According to paragraph 4, what makes bamboo commercially attractive to builders and furniture makers?
options: A. It is the cheapest building material available anywhere.
B. It matures fast on poor land, sparing scarce forests.
C. It grows on the very land used for food crops.
D. It has completely replaced tropical hardwood in furniture making.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 4: tre 'reaches maturity in a few seasons, on marginal land unsuited to food crops... without stripping ancient woodlands', trưởng thành nhanh trên đất cằn, giảm áp lực lên rừng, nên B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

In paragraph 2, the word 'commends' is closest in meaning to:
options: A. makes it attractive
B. openly praises it
C. entrusts it to others
D. sets it against something
questions.explanation: 'commends bamboo to anyone' nghĩa là làm cho tre trở nên hấp dẫn/đáng chọn (giới thiệu một cách thuận lợi), nên A đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What can be inferred from the statement that bamboo captures carbon quickly 'at least while the plants are young and growing vigorously'?
options: A. Mature bamboo releases the carbon it once stored back into the air.
B. Bamboo absorbs more carbon than any broadleaf forest on Earth.
C. Only young bamboo can absorb carbon dioxide at all.
D. Bamboo's edge in capturing carbon may fade as the plants grow older.
questions.explanation: Cụm 'at least while the plants are young and growing vigorously' hàm ý lợi thế hút carbon mạnh nhất khi cây còn non, nên có thể giảm khi cây già, D là suy luận đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

Which of the following best describes the writer's attitude toward bamboo as a timber substitute?
options: A. Unreservedly enthusiastic about its environmental benefits.
B. Broadly appreciative but wary of exaggerated green claims.
C. Skeptical that it offers any real advantage over wood.
D. Detached and factual, offering no personal judgement.
questions.explanation: Tác giả công nhận 'genuine promise' nhưng 'cautions against the sweeping claims' và cảnh báo 'environmental halo shines brighter than its actual record', trân trọng nhưng dè chừng lời thổi phồng, B đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 4

What is the main purpose of paragraph 5?
options: A. To explain in detail how bamboo boards are actually manufactured.
B. To compare bamboo's tensile strength with that of steel.
C. To balance the earlier praise by admitting the material's weaknesses.
D. To argue that bamboo should not be used in building.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 5 mở đầu 'the enthusiasm... deserves to be tempered by a clear-eyed look at its shortcomings', mục đích là nêu nhược điểm để cân bằng lời khen trước đó, nên C đúng.
